newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: We're not fat, we're artists, say sumo giants.
newsitem.headline: We're not fat, we're artists, say sumo giants.

text.p: The ancient Japanese art of sumo wrestling is tired of being called a fat man's sport.

Some of sumo's biggest stars, including the 226-kg (500 lb) Akebono, arrived in Sydney on Wednesday ahead of a goodwill tournament at the weekend and asked Australian reporters to stop focusing on their girths.
After a tournament in Melbourne last weekend, local newspapers have been full of stories on just how much the touring Sumo wrestlers eat.
One group of wrestlers went to a Gold Coast funfair, ate a A$3,000 (US$2,300) seafood meal -- and still took a ride down the rollercoaster.
Another group went to the races and, predictably enough, looked "hungry enough to eat a horse".

"I would like to ask you not just to focus on their size or eating habits but to look instead at a sport based on courtesy," Sho Sakaigawa, chairman of the Japan Sumo Association, told a news conference on Wednesday.
Akebono, born in Hawaii and the first sumo grand champion not from Japan, said the wrestlers themselves ignored reports focusing on their weight.
He said sumo was not even a sport, but an ancient art practised 24 hours a day.
"We're just here to show people what sumo is about and not how big we are and how much we eat," Akebono said.
"I just hope you get the chance to see sumo for what it is and not for what we look like."
